title: Finite State Machine
body:
A circuit with a finite set of states, a transition rule that picks the next state from
the current state and the inputs, and an output rule. In hardware it is two pieces bolted
together: [[Flip-Flop]]s holding the state, and [[Combinational Logic]] computing the next
state and the outputs from it.

```
        inputs ─┐
                ├─→ [ next-state logic ] ─→ [ flip-flops ] ─┬─→ state
   current state┘                                            │
                └────────────── feedback ────────────────────┘
```

Two flavours, and the difference is worth knowing:

| | Output depends on | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Moore** | State only | Output changes only on a clock edge, so it is glitch-free |
| **Mealy** | State **and** inputs | Reacts a cycle sooner, but an input glitch shows up on the output |

**How you build one.** Draw the state diagram → assign a bit pattern to each state →
build the [[Excitation Table]] for every transition → minimise the next-state logic (a
[[Karnaugh Maps|K-map]] job) → wire it to the flip-flops.

This is the same object [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] studies as
[[Finite Automata]], just with the emphasis moved. There the question is *what languages
can a machine with finitely many states recognise*; here it is *what does the circuit do
on the next clock edge*. Same finiteness, same lack of unbounded memory, which is why an
FSM cannot count arbitrarily high any more than a [[DFA]] can match arbitrarily nested
brackets.

A [[CPU]]'s control unit is an FSM: the [[Fetch-Execute Cycle]] is its state diagram.
